summary: Olympic National Park Aircraft Warning Service post built in fall 1942 by park staff; abandoned after the war, NRHP-listed 2007, last reported standing in 2015.

facts.design: Custom-designed single-story frame cabin with an attached storage shed (register); Wikipedia describes a 13-by-16-foot structure clad in wood shingles under a simple pitched roof
facts.status_note: Last reported standing in July 2015 by the register; the sources read give no later condition report.

access.note: Reached on foot up the Pyramid Peak trail inside Olympic National Park. The sources read do not confirm current trail or cabin conditions.

visit.trail_note: 3.5 miles up the Pyramid Peak trail from the end of Camp David Jr. Road, per the NRHP record.

events.note: Built in the fall of 1942 as an Aircraft Warning Service post; funded by the U.S. Army and built by NPS employees Joe and Rena Shurnick.
Aircraft Warning Service use ended in June 1944 per Wikipedia; firelookout.com gives 1945 as the abandonment year.
NPS coastal defense history says it was one of two WWII Aircraft Warning Service structures in the park still standing in 1983.
Added to the National Register of Historic Places on July 13, 2007.
firelookout.com records the cabin as still there in 2013.
Registered on the National Historic Lookout Register on August 30, 2015; the register says it was still standing as of July 2015.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: firelookout.com says Olympic National Forest; Wikipedia, the register and the NRHP record say Olympic National Park. The park is used.
Wikipedia gives June 1944 for the end of Aircraft Warning Service use; firelookout.com gives 1945. Not resolved; both dates are reported in the story.
The register gives 821 m (2,695 ft); firelookout.com gives 3000 ft. The register figure matches the record, so it is kept.

notes_for_editor: Current condition is unconfirmed: the newest status line is the 2015 register entry. The story leaves out a trail landslide and 2014 closure, and a claim that Wikipedia calls the summit structure restored; both appeared only in search summaries and the Wikipedia text read did not show them. The NRHP nomination PDF link returned 404, so only the NPGallery record page was read. Brief error: county spelled Challam, corrected to Clallam. The 13-by-16-foot size and pitched roof come from Wikipedia only, not the register, and Wikipedia calls that structure a 'shed'; the story now attributes them to Wikipedia. Fact-check 2026-10-08: the story's register sentence was reworded, and the Japanese-aircraft and thirteen-sites claims now have full evidence quotes.
